v.why: Raising an already large learning rate destabilizes Adam training and collapses accuracy.
At very small learning rates the network is undertrained in 243 epochs, so a larger step helps.
Lowering a too-large learning rate restores stable training.
Lowering an already tiny learning rate leaves the model undertrained.
Strong L2 penalty underfits, so weakening it recovers accuracy.
Increasing an already heavy penalty pushes the model further into underfitting.
Deeper networks are more unstable at large learning rates.
Removing a layer reduces instability when the learning rate is large.
Very large batches give few updates in a fixed epoch budget and generalize worse.
With a tiny learning rate, fewer updates from larger batches worsen undertraining.

raw:
I haven't run anything beyond the 100 provided experiments. These hypotheses rest on those measurements plus general knowledge of how Adam-trained MLPs behave. The learning-rate and alpha hypotheses have the strongest support. The batch-size and depth ones are more speculative.

- **Learning rate up at a high rate:** runs 7, 8 and 10 lost accuracy on all three datasets.
- **Learning rate up at a low rate:** runs 1 and 2 gained on all three datasets.
- **Learning rate down at a high rate:** runs 12 and 13 gained.
- **Learning rate down at a low rate:** runs 18 and 19 mostly lost accuracy.
- **Alpha down from a high alpha:** runs 31 and 40 gained on all three datasets.
- **Alpha up from a high alpha:** run 27 lost on all three datasets.
- **Depth at a high learning rate:** run 65 lost badly going deeper, and run 75 gained going shallower.
- **Batch size up at a large batch:** run 49 lost on all three datasets.
- **Batch size up at a low learning rate:** run 50 lost on all three datasets, plausibly because larger batches mean fewer updates in a fixed 243 epochs.
